title: Jaipur's Vinita Somani Cooked Through Chemotherapy, Then Trained Nearly 200 Women
excerpt: Diagnosed with breast cancer in 2011 after losing both parents and an aunt to the disease, she built a garage-kitchen hobby into Appetite, a bakery school branch, and a second career supporting other patients.
body:
• Jaipur's Vinita Somani was diagnosed with stage-two breast cancer in 2011, after losing her mother, father and maternal aunt to the disease. Between chemotherapy cycles, she taught herself cuisines from cookbooks and began teaching others in her garage kitchen.
  • Her home venture Appetite grew into cooking classes and a Jaipur branch of the School of Bakery and Culinary Arts; nearly 200 women have trained under her, and many now earn through baking and cooking businesses of their own.
  • Nearly a decade after her first diagnosis, cancer returned in her other breast at stage three. She came through a second, harder course of chemotherapy.
  • Today she also does cancer-awareness and patient-support work in Jaipur, runs the Aapbeeti Facebook community for people sharing illness and family struggles, and founded the Arpan Parv Club, a festival community of more than 70 members.

Cancer was the thing Vinita Somani feared most, because she had watched it take her family. "Cancer had always been my greatest fear because I had lost my mother, father and aunt to the disease," she said in an interview carried by The Times of India. "When I was diagnosed, I felt as though my entire world had come to a standstill." The diagnosis came in 2011: stage-two breast cancer, followed by surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy that left her weak and cost her her hair.

What pulled her forward was, at first, a family occasion. Preparations for her son's wedding gave her something absorbing to do — work with food, which she had always loved experimenting with, without ever having considered it a profession. She needed, she has said, something that would keep her mind away from the disease.

""Nothing makes me happier than knowing that women who once came to me as students are now earning through baking and cooking," she said."

A garage kitchen between chemo cycles

Between chemotherapy sessions, Somani began practising recipes in earnest, working through cookbooks — culinary author Tarla Dalal's books were among her guides — and following culinary programmes to sharpen her technique. She started teaching a few people in her garage kitchen. She also spotted a gap: Jaipur at the time offered few international cuisines, so she built her repertoire around Italian, Mexican, continental, Japanese and Chinese dishes alongside Indian cooking. People liked the food, and orders began to come in.

As demand grew, she formalised the work as Appetite, a home venture offering prepared food and cooking classes across Indian and international cuisines. Then she made the move that turned a personal recovery into other people's livelihoods: she established a Jaipur branch of the School of Bakery and Culinary Arts, aimed at women who wanted skills they could earn from independently.

Nearly 200 women trained

Over the years, nearly 200 women have trained under Somani. Many have gone on to start baking and cooking ventures of their own, earning money and contributing to their families. "Nothing makes me happier than knowing that women who once came to me as students are now earning through baking and cooking," she said. Her work has been recognised along the way: celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor honoured her cooking classes, the Jaipur Moms Group recognised her as a home chef in the city, and the Confederation of Women Entrepreneurs appreciated her enterprise. As recently as July 2026, she conducted a five-day bakery workshop for AWWA women under FICCI FLO Jaipur.

The second diagnosis

Nearly a decade after the first diagnosis, cancer was detected in her other breast — this time at stage three. The stronger chemotherapy brought prolonged fever, nausea and extreme weakness; for nearly two months, even eating was difficult, and her haemoglobin had to stay above nine to avoid delays in treatment, with iron injections adding to the discomfort. Through it, her community pushed back in the other direction: friends, students and well-wishers kept in touch, and former students sent her pictures of the food they were making — a reminder, in the middle of treatment, of the lives her teaching had already changed.

From survivor to support system

Having been through cancer twice, Somani has folded support work into her life alongside the cooking. She is involved in cancer awareness and patient-support activities through the cancer care wing associated with Jaipur's Mahavir Cancer Hospital, and her social media posts about her own experience have prompted women to reach out with questions about chemotherapy, nutrition and the fear of recurrence. Through Aapbeeti, a Facebook initiative, she gives people a space to share illnesses, family difficulties and personal struggles without fear of judgement. She is also associated with Make-A-Wish, which fulfils the wishes of critically ill children, and she founded the Arpan Parv Club, a community of more than 70 members who gather to celebrate Indian festivals.

The arc of the story is the part worth holding onto: an activity taken up to survive the worst days — cooking, between one chemotherapy cycle and the next — became a business, then a school, then a route into earning for nearly 200 other women.
